2.0.big: Life is chemistry. Everything living is built from atoms bonded into molecules, mostly carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen, in a world full of water.
points: Matter is anything that takes up space and has mass. An element is a pure substance made of one kind of atom.

2.1.big: An atom is a nucleus (protons + neutrons) surrounded by electrons. Atoms bond by sharing or transferring electrons.
points: Atomic number = number of protons (defines the element). Mass number = protons + neutrons. Neutrons = mass number − atomic number. Atomic weight = the average mass of an element's isotopes.
Isotopes = same element, different numbers of neutrons (carbon-12 vs. carbon-14). A radioisotope is unstable and decays (used for dating fossils and in medicine).
The periodic table arranges elements by atomic number. Elements in the same column behave alike.

Electrons fill electron orbitals (each orbital holds 2) in shells: 2, then 8, then 8. The electron configuration describes how they're arranged. The outer valence shell controls chemical reactivity. The octet rule: atoms want 8 outer electrons. A noble gas (inert gas) already has a full shell.
A molecule is atoms bonded together. A compound has two or more different elements.

A chemical reaction turns reactants into products. A balanced chemical equation has the same atoms on both sides. A reversible chemical reaction goes both ways and reaches equilibrium (the law of mass action: adding more reactant pushes it forward). An irreversible chemical reaction goes one way.

Chemical bonds: ionic bond (one atom gives electrons to another by electron transfer, making an ion: cation + and anion −, which attract; dissolved ions are electrolytes), covalent bond (shared electrons; the strongest), nonpolar covalent bond (shared equally), polar covalent bond (shared unequally because one atom has higher electronegativity).
Weak attractions: the hydrogen bond (a partly positive H attracted to a partly negative atom) and the van der Waals interaction. They're weak alone but hold DNA and proteins in shape.
2.1.tip: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number. Example: xenon 108 − 54 = 54 neutrons.

2.2.big: Water's special properties all come from its polarity and the hydrogen bonds between water molecules.
points: Oxygen pulls electrons harder than hydrogen, so O is slightly negative and the H's slightly positive.
Hydrophilic (water-loving) substances are polar or charged and dissolve. Hydrophobic (water-fearing) ones are nonpolar, like oils.
Ice floats because hydrogen bonds lock molecules into a spread-out lattice, so solid water is less dense. Lakes freeze from the top, insulating life below.

High specific heat capacity: water takes lots of energy to warm up, so it steadies temperatures (a calorie is the heat to raise 1 g of water by 1 °C). High heat of vaporization of water: evaporation of sweat carries away lots of heat.
Water is a great solvent: it surrounds ions with a sphere of hydration, causing dissociation.
Cohesion (water sticks to water) causes surface tension, so insects can walk on it. Adhesion (water sticks to other things) plus cohesion drives capillary action up thin tubes like plant xylem.
pH scale: 0–14. Below 7 = acid (gives off H⁺). Above 7 = base (takes up H⁺ or gives off OH⁻). Each step is 10× different. Test with litmus paper or pH paper.
Buffers soak up extra H⁺ or OH⁻ to keep pH steady. The bicarbonate system buffers blood.

2.3.big: Carbon is the backbone of life because it can form four covalent bonds, building chains, branches and rings.
points: Organic molecules contain carbon (and hydrogen). A hydrocarbon is just C and H. Aliphatic hydrocarbons are chains. Aromatic hydrocarbons have rings. A substituted hydrocarbon has other groups attached.

Isomers: same formula, different arrangement. Structural isomers have different bonding. Geometric isomers (cis/trans) differ around a double bond. Enantiomers are mirror images, needing a carbon with four different groups attached.
Saturated fats: all single bonds, straight chains, solid at room temperature. Unsaturated fats: double bonds cause kinks, liquid.

Functional groups give molecules their chemistry: hydroxyl (–OH, polar), carbonyl (C=O), carboxyl (–COOH, releases H⁺, acidic; in amino acids and fatty acids), amino (–NH₂, basic), phosphate (–PO₄, in DNA and ATP), sulfhydryl (–SH), methyl (–CH₃, nonpolar).

2.why: 19 electrons: 2 + 8 + 8 = 18, so shells 1–3 are full and shell 4 has 1.

4.why: False: in water, ionic bonds break apart, so they're weaker than covalent bonds.

6.why: Ionic bonds form between ions with opposite charges.

7.why: Cl (3.16) pulls harder than H (2.20), so H is partly positive and Cl partly negative. (LiF's charges are also right; it's ionic.)

8.why: False: nitrogen (N₂) is the most abundant molecule in the atmosphere.

9.why: Oxygen is more electronegative, so electrons sit closer to it, making O partly negative.

10.why: Adding acid adds H⁺, so pH drops.

15.why: Enantiomers need four different groups on a central carbon.

16.why: Sodium is an ion, not a functional group.

19.why: Both have 6 protons (atomic number 6). Mass numbers are 13 and 12.

20.why: Their many weak attractions hold DNA and proteins in their working shapes.

21.why: Group 1 gives up 1 electron easily and Group 17 needs 1: a strong ionic pair (like NaCl).

23.why: Buffers absorb extra H⁺ and OH⁻. Example: the bicarbonate system in blood.

24.why: Ice is less dense and floats, water has a high specific heat, and a high heat of vaporization makes sweating cool you.

25.why: 0–14, with below 7 acidic and above 7 basic. Bicarbonate buffers blood.

26.why: Up to 4 bonds, so carbon can build long chains.

27.why: Carboxyl groups release H⁺. They're in amino acids and fatty acids.

28.why: Saturated = single bonds, solid. Unsaturated = double bonds, liquid.

29.why: High specific heat capacity keeps body temperature steady.

30.why: Cohesion (water–water: surface tension), adhesion (water–other: capillary action in plants), heat of vaporization (liquid → gas: sweating cools).
